title: Wyckoff Spring
teaches: The Wyckoff spring as we teach it: in a leader above its 200-day, resting in a flat sideways range, price dips a little under the floor and closes back inside. We read the range, the depth of the dip (0.1 to 1 ATR) and the close, buy the reclaim or the later quiet test, put the stop a few cents under the spring low, and take the stop as the trade, because a spring that fails usually fails at once. A single swing low is a 2B, a rising average is an undercut and rally, and a dip of 2 ATR or more is a breakdown.

steps: Here's the hard one. MSFT, August 2023: a 40-day range, 324.41 to 366.78, three touches of the floor.
August 8 it probes just under the floor to 323.00 on light volume. Everything we want is there.
Next day, buy at market, 326.47. Stop 322.97, 1.07% away. That same session it trades 321.05 and closes 322.23.
Stopped out on the entry day. A spring that fails usually fails right away. Take the small loss and move on.

questions.q: Wyckoff traders talk about a spring inside a sideways range. What actually happens on a spring?
choices: Price dips under the floor, snaps back
Price breaks over the top and holds
Price slides through the floor slowly
Price closes under the floor, stays
questions.answer: Price dips under the floor, snaps back
questions.why: It dips under the floor and snaps right back inside. That's a spring. Everyone can see that floor, so stops and nervous sellers sit just under it. The dip runs them, nothing follows, and price is right back in the box. Speed is the tell. Pruden's spring quickly reverses back into the range. Taylor calls a slow slide that fails a washout or a bear trap. Slow means sellers had real control. Fast means they got trapped.
questions.lesson_line: A spring dips under the floor and snaps right back inside.

wrong.Price breaks over the top and holds: That's a breakout over resistance. A spring happens at the bottom of the range, under the floor.
wrong.Price slides through the floor slowly: Too slow. A spring snaps back quickly. A slow slide that fails is a washout or a bear trap.
wrong.Price closes under the floor, stays: That's a breakdown. On a spring, price gets right back inside the range.

questions.simple: A quick dip under the range floor that gets right back inside.

reasons: three publishers agree (Pruden, ChartSchool, Taylor); a stable definition

questions.q: A spring takes price below the low of a range and then closes back inside the range.
questions.why: True. A spring takes price below the low of the range, then reverses and closes within it.
questions.lesson_line: Under the floor, then back inside the range.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: A spring is bought at the floor on the ___ after the undercut.
questions.why: Reclaim. A spring is bought at the floor on the reclaim after the undercut, with the stop under the dip.
questions.lesson_line: Buy the reclaim at the floor, not the breakout at the top.

questions.q: A stock has built a sideways range for weeks. When in that range do Wyckoff traders expect the spring to show up?
choices: Late, once the floor is set
On the first day of the range
questions.answer: Late, once the floor is set
questions.why: Late. The floor has to earn it first. A level that's held again and again is one everybody watches, and that's the one worth undercutting. Pruden's reason is the useful part. The late dip is the market's final test of the supply left. If that test comes up empty, the range is ready to go. Fraser and ChartSchool put it late too. It's a tendency though, not a day count.
questions.lesson_line: A spring comes late, after the floor has proven itself.

wrong.On the first day of the range: There's no floor yet on day one. A floor has to be tested before a dip under it means anything.
wrong.Any time, there's no pattern: There is one. ChartSchool, Fraser and Pruden all put the spring late in the range.
wrong.Only after the top breaks: That's after the range is over. The spring comes late inside the range, at the floor.

questions.simple: Late in the range, after the floor has been tested enough to matter.

questions.q: On a spring buy, your stop goes a few cents under the low of the dip.
questions.why: True. The low of the dip is your line. If price goes back under it, the spring failed and you want out. A few cents under, not right on it, so a tick to the exact low doesn't shake you out. Don't use the old floor. It sits above the dip's low, so the same wiggle that made the spring takes you out. Same stop if you buy the test instead.
questions.lesson_line: Stop a few cents under the spring low. That's where you're wrong.
questions.simple: True, a few cents under the low of the dip, because that's where the spring has failed.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, F62)

questions.q: How tall is a spring's range, floor to top?
questions.why: 6% to 20%, measured from the floor to the top. That band is on our setup card. A range over 20% is not ruled out; it grades lower. A range much tighter than 6% falls short of it.
questions.lesson_line: A spring range is 6% to 20% tall.

wrong.1% to 3%: Too small. Our card asks for a range 6% to 20% tall, floor to top.
wrong.30% to 50%: Over 20% grades lower. This is far past it.
wrong.3% to 6%: Our card's band is 6% to 20%, floor to top. This sits under it.

questions.simple: A spring's range should be 6% to 20% tall, from the floor to the top.

reasons: proposed card criterion, the owner's review pending

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: On our card, a dip over ___ ATR under the floor is a shakeout that grades lower.
questions.why: 1. On our card a dip over 1 ATR under the floor is a shakeout, and it grades lower. A full spring dips at least 0.1 ATR and at most about 1 ATR. Over 2 ATR is a breakdown, not a spring.
questions.lesson_line: A real undercut, but no deeper than about 1 ATR.
questions.simple: Over 1 ATR under the floor, the dip is a shakeout that grades lower.

reasons: proposed card criterion (spr.dip_depth), the owner's review pending

questions.q: A stock drops 3 ATR under its range floor in one day on heavy selling. That's still a spring.
questions.why: False. That's not a dip under the floor, that's sellers running it right through. A spring is a small undercut that snaps back. A drop of 3 ATR is about three normal days of movement gone in one session. A stop under that low would also sit a long way from any sane buy. Fraser calls this kind of complete breakdown his number 1 spring, and he says don't buy it.
questions.lesson_line: A spring scratches the floor. A breakdown goes right through it.
questions.simple: False. A drop that big is a breakdown, not a quick dip that snaps back.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting the owner's review (the ATR bands)

questions.q: You're scanning for springs. What RS rating should the stock carry before you even care about the pattern?
questions.why: 80 or more. We buy leaders, stocks in the strongest groups that have been beating the market. A spring is a shakeout inside a strong stock's rest. In a weak stock the same dip is just the next leg down. So check the RS Rating on the chart in our app first, then look at the pattern. The only trades we let off this rule are parabolic and mean-reversion ones.
questions.lesson_line: Leaders spring. Weak stocks just break.

wrong.20 or less, a beaten-down name: That's one of the weakest stocks out there. Its dip under a floor is more likely the next leg down.
wrong.Around 50, an average stock: Average isn't a leader. We want 80 or more.
wrong.Any rating, the pattern's enough: The pattern only works in a leader. The RS rating comes first.

questions.simple: 80 or more, because a spring only works in a leader that's been beating the market.

questions.q: A stock dips under its range floor in the morning and closes back inside, up near the day's high. That close is a good sign.
questions.why: True. Where it closes tells you who won the day. Sellers pushed it under the floor, and buyers took it all back by the close. A close up near the high says demand showed up and stayed. A close back under the spring low is the opposite, and that one you don't buy. I want to see the day finish strong, not limp back in.
questions.lesson_line: Where it closes tells you who won the day.
questions.simple: True, a close near the high shows buyers took the whole dip back and held it.

reasons: proposed card criterion (spr.reclaim_close), the owner's review pending

questions.q: A clean spring is on your list. Which readings on our market filter (Green, Yellow, Orange, Red) suit buying it?
questions.why: Green or Yellow. A spring is a bet that the shakeout fails and buyers win. That's a lot easier with the market behind you. Green means full risk for the grade. Yellow means smaller and fewer. In Orange we only take an A+, and Red is mostly cash for us. The reading is a guide, not a switch, but it sets how hard you press.
questions.lesson_line: Let the market tell you how hard to press.

wrong.Orange or Red, any grade: Orange is A+ only, and Red is mostly cash. Neither is a spot for an ordinary spring.
wrong.Red, when fear peaks: Red is mostly cash for us. Fear at its peak can get worse first.
wrong.Any reading, chart decides: A clean chart doesn't override the market. The reading sets how much you trade.

questions.simple: Green or Yellow, because a spring needs buyers to show up, and that's easier when the market is healthy.

questions.q: GIS spent 12 weeks between 21.30 and 23.30, tapping the floor four times. What makes a range like that flat?
choices: No clear slope up or down
questions.answer: No clear slope up or down
questions.why: No clear slope. The highs and lows go sideways, and the floor keeps holding in the same spot. That's what makes the floor mean something. Sellers showed up at the top and buyers at the bottom, again and again. A range that slopes is a trend, not a floor. You judge flat by eye: draw the floor and the top, and see if price stays in the box.
questions.lesson_line: Draw the box. If price stays in it, it's flat.

wrong.A higher high every week: That's a stair-step up, a trend. Flat goes sideways.
wrong.Its height is small: Height and slope are different things. A tight range can still slope.
wrong.Volume dries up through it: Nice to see, and it raises the grade. But flat is about price going sideways.

questions.simple: Flat means no clear slope, price going sideways in a box with a floor that keeps holding.

reasons: proposed card criterion (spr.flat), the owner's review pending

questions.q: A clean spring triggers Tuesday. The company reports Thursday, two days out. You can take the buy.
questions.why: False. Two days out is inside our window. We make no new buys in the 3 days before a report. A report can gap a stock right through your stop, and no chart pattern protects you from that. Pass for now and look again after the report. The rule is about new buys. A trade already up 5R may be held through one.
questions.lesson_line: No new buys in the 3 days before a report.
questions.simple: False. Two days before a report is too close, because the report can gap it through your stop.

questions.q: Wyckoff's advice, as Pruden writes it, is to buy a range when price breaks out over the top.
questions.why: False. Pruden writes that, per Wyckoff, you shouldn't buy breakouts. A false breakout leaves you open to a fast move the other way. The spring is the answer to that. You buy down at the floor, after the shakeout fails, with the stop just under the low. Your risk is small, and the whole range sits above you as room.
questions.lesson_line: Buy the spring at the floor, not the breakout at the top.
questions.simple: False. Wyckoff warned against buying breakouts, so we buy a spring down at the floor.

deeper.counter: Some scanners buy over the range top but keep the stop under the spring low. That's the worst of both. The stop ends up the whole range away from the buy, so your size shrinks and the reward for the risk falls apart. A spring is bought at the floor.

reasons: the Wyckoff line rests on one publisher (Pruden), so it is asked as his
the floor entry rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting the owner's review (spr.not_breakout_entry)

questions.q: Floor 91.25, top 100.68. How much room is that, floor to top, as a percent of the floor?
questions.why: 10.3%. 100.68 minus 91.25 is 9.43. Divide that by the floor, 91.25, and you get 10.3%. That's your room. The top of the range is the first place sellers show up, so it's the first spot the move can stall. Buy near the floor with a tight stop and 10.3% of room is plenty of R to work with. Measure off the floor, since that's where you're buying.
questions.lesson_line: Top minus floor, over the floor. That's your room to the ceiling.
questions.simple: The range is 10.3% tall, so there's about that much room from the floor up to the top.

reasons: proposed card criterion (spr.range_height), the owner's review pending

wrong.9.4%: You divided by the top. Measure off the floor, where you buy.
wrong.110.3%: That's the top as a share of the floor, not the room between them.
wrong.1.0%: The decimal point slipped a place.

questions.story: December 2020. This stock just closed back inside its range after one close under the floor. You're looking at a buy near the floor.

questions.q: The floor is 150.00 and ATR is 3.00. The dip bottoms at 149.10, then closes back inside. How deep was it, in ATR?
questions.why: 0.3 ATR. 150.00 minus 149.10 is 0.9 under the floor. Divide by the 3.00 ATR and you get 0.3. ATR sizes the dip against a normal day for this stock. A third of a normal day's range is a scratch under the floor, not a break. And a shallow dip keeps your stop, a few cents under 149.10, close to where you buy.
questions.lesson_line: Dollars under the floor, divided by the ATR.
questions.simple: 0.3 ATR, because 0.9 under the floor divided by an ATR of 3.00 is 0.3.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting the owner's review (0.1 to 1 ATR)

wrong.0.9 ATR: That's the dollars under the floor. You still have to divide by the 3.00 ATR.
wrong.3.3 ATR: Flipped the division, ATR over the dollars.
wrong.0.6 ATR: That's the percent under the floor, not the ATR.

questions.q: Fraser numbers his springs 1 to 3. A shallow dip under the prior low, on modest volume: which one is it?
questions.why: Number 3. Fraser's number 3 is the shallow dip on modest volume, and he says you can buy it right away. His number 2 goes deeper on heavier volume and needs a test before you buy. Number 1 is a complete breakdown, never bought. Watch out, the numbers run backwards: 3 is the good one. For us, volume only raises the grade. It's never a must.
questions.lesson_line: Fraser's number 3: shallow, quiet, and you can buy it.

wrong.A test on high volume: A test comes after the spring, and a good one is lighter, not heavier.
wrong.A number 1 spring: Fraser's number 1 is a complete breakdown. You don't buy it.
wrong.A number 2 spring: Fraser's number 2 goes deeper on expanded volume, then needs a test.

questions.simple: A number 3 spring, the shallow quiet one Fraser says you can buy right away.

deeper.trap: Fraser's numbers run backwards: number 1 is the deepest and the worst, a breakdown not to buy, and number 3 is the shallow one you can buy. And quiet is not settled. Taylor, a CMT member, wants volume on the spring quite high, the higher the better. Treat the volume read as the Wyckoff school's view, not a fact.

reasons: tied to the held volume decision D-006

questions.q: Your stock sprang and closed back inside. Next day, before you've bought, it closes back under the spring low. You skip it.
questions.why: True. Pass on this one. A spring only works if that low holds. A close back under it says the shakeout wasn't a shakeout. The sellers came back. Buy it there and you're buying a breakdown. Let it go and wait for a new range to form. Taylor puts it plainly: if the spring low gets violated by any real degree, the structure is invalidated.
questions.lesson_line: If the spring low breaks before you buy, there's no trade.
questions.simple: True. A close back under the spring low means the spring failed, so there's nothing to buy.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting the owner's review (spr.inv_close_under_low)

questions.q: Leaders often shake out under more than the range floor. Besides the floor, what does a spring often dip through?
questions.why: The 20 EMA or the 50-day. A shakeout under the floor often takes out a fast average too. That's normal, leaders do it. It flushes the people using those lines as stops, then price comes right back. The 200-day is different. Below it is a hard no for stocks. A spring is a scratch under a floor inside an uptrend, not a collapse.
questions.lesson_line: A shakeout through the 20 or the 50 is normal. Under the 200-day is a no.

wrong.A new multi-year low: That's a collapse. A spring is a small dip under a flat floor.
wrong.Nothing but the floor: Leaders often shake out under the 20 EMA or the 50-day as well.
wrong.The 200-day line: Below the 200-day is a hard no for stocks. A spring lives above it.

questions.simple: The 20 EMA or the 50-day, which leaders often shake out under, but never the 200-day.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26) and sits beside the held D-009

questions.q: Any dip under a recent low counts as a spring, even with no range behind it.
questions.why: False. A falling stock makes a new low every day. With no real range behind the dip, that is not a spring.
questions.lesson_line: No range, no spring.

questions.q: What are you looking at?
questions.story: October 2001. A flat 12-week range, 9.4% tall, floor tapped four times. One day it dips 0.13 ATR under the floor and closes back inside.
questions.why: That's a spring, and a clean one. The floor's been tapped four times, so everyone can see it. The dip under it was 0.13 ATR, barely a scratch. Then it closed right back inside the same day. Sellers had their shot under an obvious floor and nothing came of it. That was GIS, and it ran straight through the ceiling after.
questions.lesson_line: Flat floor, tiny scratch under it, back inside the same day. That's a spring.

wrong.A flat-base breakout: A breakout goes over the top. This one dipped under the floor.
wrong.A breakdown of the floor: A breakdown keeps going and closes under. This was a scratch that closed back inside.
wrong.A 2B of a single low: A 2B is one swing low. This floor was tapped four times.

questions.simple: A spring, because a flat range got a tiny dip under its floor that closed right back inside.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting the owner's review (height, depth, close)

questions.q: Spring or not?
choices: No, there's no range behind it
questions.story: A stock has made a new low every day for two weeks. Today it ticks up and closes above yesterday's low.
questions.answer: No, there's no range behind it
questions.why: Not a spring. There's no floor here. A stock making a new low every day has no level for a spring to dip under. One up day in a downtrend is just a bounce. A spring needs a sideways range first, with a floor that's held a few times. Volume isn't your issue. The missing range is.
questions.lesson_line: No floor, no spring.

wrong.Yes, it bounced right back: A bounce in a downtrend isn't a spring. There's no floor to reclaim.
wrong.Yes, any reclaimed dip counts: A spring needs a flat range behind the dip. This one has none.
wrong.No, the volume looks wrong: Volume isn't the problem. The missing range is.

questions.simple: No, because a stock falling to a new low every day has no floor to spring off.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting the owner's review (spr.inv_no_range)

questions.q: Is that a spring you can buy?
choices: No, it was too slow to come back
Yes, six days is a deep test
No, it had to hold the 50-day
questions.story: A stock closes under its range floor six sessions in a row. On the seventh day it closes back inside.
questions.answer: No, it was too slow to come back
questions.why: No. A spring snaps back. Six closes under the floor is a slow slide. Pruden's spring quickly reverses back into the range, and Taylor calls slow failures like this washouts or bear traps. Here's why it matters. The fast reclaim is what tells you sellers got trapped. Six days under means they had control for over a week. I'm not counting days exactly, I'm looking for the snap.
questions.lesson_line: A spring snaps back. Six closes under is a slide.

wrong.Yes, it closed back inside: Closing back inside is half of it. The reversal also has to be quick.
wrong.Yes, six days is a deep test: A test comes after a spring. Six closes under is a slow violation.
wrong.No, it had to hold the 50-day: Nothing here says where the 50-day is, and leaders often shake out under it.

questions.simple: No, because a spring snaps back fast, and six closes under the floor is a slow slide.

reasons: the reclaim window is a held decision (D-005); only 'quickly reverses' is keyed

questions.q: How would you grade it?
questions.story: January 2021. The floor is 359.50. The dip goes 1.34 ATR under it and closes under for a day, then closes back inside the next day.
questions.why: A shakeout, and I'd grade it lower. It came back, so it's not a breakdown. But 1.34 ATR is a real drop, and it closed under the floor for a day before it got back in. Sellers had control for a full session. That's sloppier than a quick scratch. And look at the 50-day, pointed down right overhead. One more reason it grades lower. You can still trade it, just smaller. COST was bought at 361.30 with the stop at 352.41, 2.46% away. It made 0.52R and got stopped.
questions.lesson_line: The deeper and slower the dip, the lower the grade.

wrong.A clean spring, full grade: A clean spring is a quick scratch. This went 1.34 ATR under and sat there a day.
wrong.A breakdown, don't buy it: A breakdown keeps going. This one closed back inside the next day.
wrong.An undercut and rally: That uses a rising average or one swing low. This level is a flat floor.

questions.simple: A shakeout that grades lower, because the dip was deep and sat under the floor a day before it came back.

deeper.example: COST: the floor was 359.50 and the probe went 1.34 ATR under it. The buy was 361.30 with the stop at 352.41, a 2.46% stop. It made 0.52R and was stopped. A deeper dip puts the stop further from the buy.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting the owner's review (1 and 2 ATR bands)

questions.q: Where's your stop?
choices: A few cents under the spring low
Near 5% under the buy, for room
A few cents under the floor
questions.story: May 2015. You bought at 150.40 the morning after the dip. The floor is 149.53, and the dip went 0.15 ATR under it.
questions.answer: A few cents under the spring low
questions.why: A few cents under the spring low. In the real trade that was 149.09, 0.87% under the 150.40 buy. The low of the dip is where the spring fails, so that's where you're wrong. The 149.53 floor sits above that low. Put the stop there and the same kind of wiggle that made the spring takes you out. Then set it as a real stop order with your broker.
questions.lesson_line: The stop goes under the spring low, not the old floor.

wrong.Right on the 149.53 floor: The floor sits above the dip's low. A stop there is inside the dip's noise.
wrong.Near 5% under the buy, for room: That's extra risk for nothing. The chart says you're wrong just under the spring low, 0.87% away.
wrong.A few cents under the floor: 149.53 is the old floor, above the spring low. Go under the low of the dip.

questions.simple: A few cents under the spring low, because that's where the spring fails, not at the old floor.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, F62, D41)

questions.q: How far is your stop, as a percent of the buy?
questions.why: 1.15%. 155.40 minus 153.62 is 1.78 a share. Divide that by 155.40 and you get 1.15%. That's inside the 1-3% we like. A tight stop like that is the whole appeal of a spring. You're buying right at the floor, so the line where you're wrong is close. This one reached 3R in 8 days.
questions.lesson_line: Buy minus stop, over the buy. A spring gives you a tight one.
questions.simple: The stop is 1.15% under the buy, right inside the 1-3% we like.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A13) and the held stop-width decision D-022

wrong.1.78%: That's the dollar gap, 1.78 a share. You still divide it by the buy.
wrong.11.45%: The decimal point slipped a place.
wrong.98.85%: That's the stop as a share of the buy, not the distance.

questions.story: August 2017. You bought at the open the day after the dip at 155.40, stop at 153.62 under the spring low.

questions.q: Do you take it?
choices: Pass, Red is mostly cash for us
Buy it, the chart is clean
Half size with a tighter stop
questions.story: A clean spring in a stock above its 200-day. Our market filter, the app's Green to Red reading, is Red.
questions.answer: Pass, Red is mostly cash for us
questions.why: Pass. Red is mostly cash for us. A spring needs buyers to show up after the shakeout, and in a Red market the market isn't backing anything. The reading is a guide, but Red means sit on your hands. A clean chart doesn't change that, and neither does a smaller size. Shorting it is out too. We only short below the 200-day, and this one is above it.
questions.lesson_line: The market comes before the chart.

wrong.Buy it, the chart is clean: A clean chart doesn't beat the market. Red is mostly cash.
wrong.Pass, and short it instead: We only short below the 200-day. This stock is above it.
wrong.Half size with a tighter stop: Smaller size doesn't change the market. Keep it on your list for a better one.

questions.simple: Pass, because Red means mostly cash for us, and a clean chart doesn't change that.

deeper.trap: The trap is a perfect chart. The market reading comes first. Springs are Green or Yellow trades, and Red is mostly cash.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F65) and the card's market row

questions.q: What's the index telling you?
choices: Size up, the leader is stronger
The turn is in, QQQ sprang
questions.story: A leader springs off its range floor. QQQ sprang the same day. Before you buy, QQQ closes back under its own spring low.
questions.why: The turn hasn't come. QQQ's own spring just failed when it closed back under its low. Wyckoff's step is to time your buy with a turn in the market index. The leader's candle looks great, a hammer closing near its high. Doesn't matter. When the index can't hold its spring, the leader's spring is fighting the whole market. AAPL and QQQ sprang the same day, and both failed. I want the index behind me before I put money in.
questions.lesson_line: Check the index before you buy a leader's spring.

wrong.Nothing, only the stock matters: The index matters. Wyckoff times the buy with a turn in the market.
wrong.Size up, the leader is stronger: A failing index spring is a warning, not a reason to press.
wrong.The turn is in, QQQ sprang: QQQ's spring failed when it closed back under its low. No turn yet.

questions.simple: The market hasn't turned yet, because the index's own spring just failed.

deeper.example: AAPL and QQQ sprang on the same day in our data, and both failed. The scan scored the QQQ spring 0.0R. The index's own spring had not held, so the leader had no market turn to ride.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting the owner's review (spr.index_sprung)

questions.q: What do you take from it?
choices: The setup is broken; quit it
questions.story: A 0.16 ATR dip on light volume in a 40-day range with three touches. A 1% stop. It is stopped on the entry day with no profit.
questions.why: A spring that fails usually fails at once. 41% broke their low before any test came. The stop under the spring low is the exit.
questions.lesson_line: The stop is the trade, not a formality.

wrong.The setup is broken; quit it: One failed spring is the cost of the setup. 41% broke their low before any test.
wrong.The stop was too tight: The stop sat under the spring low, where it belongs.

questions.q: What's the play?
choices: Skip it, take it off the list
Buy it, the shape is perfect
Buy half size until it settles
Keep it on the list for later
questions.story: A textbook spring in a leader. Then a report hits that the company may be bought out.
questions.answer: Skip it, take it off the list
questions.why: Skip it and take it off the list. A buyout report changes what moves the stock. It trades on the deal now, not on buyers and sellers in the range. One headline can gap it either way, and your stop can't help you there. A perfect chart doesn't change that. As soon as there's buyout news, it comes off the list.
questions.lesson_line: Buyout news, off the list.

wrong.Keep it on the list for later: Off the list means off. Buyout news ends it.
wrong.Buy it, the shape is perfect: The shape stopped mattering when the buyout news hit. The deal moves it now.
wrong.Buy half size until it settles: Off the list means no buy at any size.

questions.simple: Skip it, because buyout news means the stock trades on the deal, not the chart.

reasons: rests on the owner's published hard rule (u04) and the card

questions.q: A spring triggers, but the stock has run well above its 9 EMA. How far above it is too stretched to buy?
questions.why: More than 10% above the 9 EMA, and we skip it. A stock that far over its fast average is stretched. Buy there and your stop is a long way back, so your size shrinks. A stretched stock also often comes back in toward the average, right into your stop. On a spring this rarely bites. You're buying near the bottom of a range, close to the averages.
questions.lesson_line: More than 10% over the 9 EMA, skip it.

wrong.More than 1% above it: Far too tight. A healthy stock sits a little above its 9 EMA all the time.
wrong.More than 25% above it: Way past our line. Over 10% is already too stretched.
wrong.There's no limit on it: There is one: more than 10% over the 9 EMA, we skip it.

questions.simple: Past 10% above the 9 EMA it's too stretched, so you skip it.

questions.q: What is wrong with that plan?
choices: The stop is far from the entry
questions.story: The scanner says to buy the range-top breakout and put the stop under the spring low.
questions.answer: The stop is far from the entry
questions.why: The stop is far from the entry. That plan had a median 12.5% stop and only 1% reached 3R. Wyckoff also says not to buy breakouts.
questions.lesson_line: Buy at the floor. A breakout buy leaves the stop far away.

wrong.The stop is too tight: It is the opposite. The stop sits far under a breakout entry.
wrong.Breakouts never work: Some do. The problem is the distance to the stop.
wrong.The range is too flat: A flat range is what we want.

questions.q: You bought a spring 10 trading days ago and it's still under 1R. You sell it.
questions.why: True. That's our time stop. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days gets sold. A good spring should go once the shakeout fails. If it just sits, your money is stuck in something that isn't working. Free it up for a setup that is. This is separate from your price stop under the spring low.
questions.lesson_line: Ten days and under 1R, sell it and move on.
questions.simple: True. After 10 days under 1R it isn't working, so you free the money.

questions.q: Your spring breaks back under its low. Buying more down there to average your cost is fine.
questions.why: False. The spring low breaking means you're out, not buying more. The stop under that low is your exit, and its whole job is to get you out when the spring fails. We buy the full size at one price with one stop, and we never add to a loser. That turns one small loss into a big one.
questions.lesson_line: A broken spring low means out, not more.
questions.simple: False. When the spring low breaks your stop takes you out, and we never add to a loser.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, A5)

questions.q: Do you sell any here?
choices: Hold, day 1 is too early to sell
Sell a third, move stop to 64.00
Sell half, leave the stop alone
questions.story: You bought at 64.00 with a stop at 62.40. On the buy day itself, price runs to 68.80, which is 3R.
questions.answer: Hold, day 1 is too early to sell
questions.why: Hold. We very rarely sell on day 1, and we usually wait until day 3 at the earliest. 3R in a day means this thing has power. Sell a chunk now and you cap your best trades. I'd rather let it run into a 3, 5 or 7 day push and sell into that. The first sell is a judgment, not a fixed third at 3R.
questions.lesson_line: Don't sell your best trade on day 1.

wrong.Sell a third, move stop to 64.00: That's the old fixed third at 3R. The first sell is a judgment, and day 1 is rarely the day.
wrong.Sell half, leave the stop alone: Selling on day 1 is rare for us. We usually wait until day 3 at the earliest.
wrong.Add more at 68.80 on strength: Not the plan. The full size went on at one price with one stop. Adding on strength is rare, a feel call.

questions.simple: Hold, because we rarely sell on day 1 and the first sell is a judgment, not a fixed 3R.

deeper.counter: A day-based push can run far past 3R. A 3, 5 or 7 day push may be 10, 12 or 20R, so a fixed third at 3R can leave most of the move behind.

questions.q: You've sold some of your spring into a push. How do you trail what's left?
choices: Under the 20 EMA, or 9 EMA if fast
Leave it under the spring low
questions.answer: Under the 20 EMA, or 9 EMA if fast
questions.why: Under the 20 EMA, or the 9 EMA if it's running fast. You sell what's left on a close below it. Most springs move at a steady pace, so the 20 EMA fits them. A rising average follows the move up and gives the trend room to breathe. Leave the stop down at the spring low and you give back the whole move. The 200-day is far too slow.
questions.lesson_line: Trail the 20 EMA. Switch to the 9 when it really runs.

wrong.Under the 200-day line: Far too slow. You'd give back most of the move before it sold.
wrong.A fixed 3% under your entry: A fixed stop doesn't follow the move up. The trail rides a rising average.
wrong.Leave it under the spring low: That's your first stop. Leave it there and you give back the whole move.

questions.simple: Under the 20 EMA, or the 9 EMA for a fast mover, and sell on a close below it.

questions.q: In our scan, about how far was the range top from a reclaim entry, at the median?
questions.why: About 4.8R, the median in our scan, and 3R or more 72% of the time. The range top is the first resistance, so 3R usually comes at or before it. It is a median, not a promise: some range tops sit closer than 3R.
questions.lesson_line: The range top is the first resistance, often past 3R.

wrong.About 3R, right at the mark: The median in our scan is 4.8R, past the 3R mark. 72% of the time it is 3R or more.
wrong.About 1.6R, before the 3R mark: The median is 4.8R, and 72% of the time it is 3R or more.
wrong.About 9.6R, far past that mark: The median in our scan is 4.8R, not 9.6R.

questions.simple: In our scan the range top sat a median 4.8R away, so 3R usually comes first.

reasons: a scan statistic that a recheck can change

questions.q: What now?
questions.story: You bought at 100.00 with a stop at 98.00. News hits overnight and it gaps down. The first 30-minute low is 95.00.
questions.why: Get out. On a gap through the stop, the first 30-minute low becomes your new stop. But there's a ceiling. Past 2R, you're done. Your risk was 2 a share, 100.00 minus 98.00. The 95.00 low is 5 under your buy. 5 over 2 is 2.5R, past the cap. The rule is there so a gap can't turn a planned loss into a disaster.
questions.lesson_line: A gap gets 30 minutes, and never more than 2R.

wrong.Buy more at 95.00 to average: That's adding to a loser. Full size at one price with one stop.
wrong.New stop at 95.00, the 30-min low: That's the gap rule without its ceiling. 2.5R is past 2R, so you're out.
wrong.Hold, it should bounce back: Hoping isn't a plan. On a gap, the 30-minute low and the 2R cap decide.

questions.simple: Get out, because the gap took the loss to 2.5R, past our 2R cap.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B20, A4)

questions.q: What do you do at the open?
choices: Weigh selling some into the gap
Sell a third, the gap forces it
Sell the whole thing at the open
Add more at 57.50 on the gap
questions.story: You bought at 50.00 with a stop at 48.00. It's day 3, and you're thinking about a first sell near 56.00, 3R. The stock opens at 57.50.
questions.answer: Weigh selling some into the gap
questions.why: Weigh selling some into it. It's day 3, the earliest we usually sell, and it opened past your level. A gap up past a sell level isn't an automatic sell though. Selling part into a big gap is a fine choice. So is letting it run and selling into the push later. It's your call, never a rule.
questions.lesson_line: A gap past your level is a chance to sell, never an order.

wrong.Add more at 57.50 on the gap: A gap past your level is a spot to sell, not buy. Adding is rare, a feel call.
wrong.Sell a third, the gap forces it: No gap forces a sell. Selling part into it is your call.
wrong.Sell the whole thing at the open: The first sell is part of the position. The rest keeps working.

questions.simple: Weigh selling some, because a gap past your level is a chance to sell, never a rule.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F63, B19)

questions.q: Volume on the spring day: do the Wyckoff writers agree on what they want to see?
choices: Yes, they all want it loud
Yes, they all want it quiet
questions.why: They don't agree. Fraser's number 3, the one he buys right away, comes on modest volume. A loud one he wants tested first. Taylor says volume on the spring is typically quite high, the higher the better. So don't turn either view into a rule. For us, volume only raises the grade. It's never the reason to buy or to pass.
questions.lesson_line: The writers split on volume. For us it raises the grade, that's all.

wrong.Yes, they all want it loud: Fraser buys the modest-volume spring right away.
wrong.Yes, they all want it quiet: Taylor wants volume on the spring high, the higher the better.
wrong.No, Fraser loud, Taylor quiet: Backwards. Fraser buys the quiet one, and Taylor wants it loud.

questions.simple: No, Fraser wants it quiet and Taylor wants it loud, so volume is a plus for us, not a rule.

deeper.trap: Do not turn one author's view into a rule. Fraser sorts springs by volume: a quiet number 3 he buys at once, a loud number 2 he waits to see tested. Taylor wants the loud one. This lesson keys only that they disagree.

reasons: volume is a held decision (D-006); only the disagreement is keyed

questions.q: A stock springs under its floor on huge volume, a deep loud flush. What do Wyckoff traders wait for before buying?
choices: A test that holds a higher low
A gap up on heavy volume
questions.answer: A test that holds a higher low
questions.why: Wait for the test. A loud, deep flush means a lot of sellers showed up. You want proof they're done before you put money in. The test is that proof. Price comes back down toward the low on lighter volume and holds a higher low. That's your buy, with the stop a few cents under the spring low. Fraser says high volume springs need to be tested. Pruden calls the test a better buy than the spring itself.
questions.lesson_line: After a loud spring, let it prove itself on the test.

wrong.A gap up on heavy volume: That's chasing. The Wyckoff buy is the quiet test, not a gap.
wrong.The 200-day to turn up: The line isn't the test. The test is a pullback that holds above the spring low.
wrong.The next earnings report: A report isn't a test. And we make no new buys in the 3 days before one.

questions.simple: A test, because after a loud flush you want proof the sellers are done, a higher low on less volume.

deeper.trap: A test that breaks the spring low is not a test that held. Taylor says the spring low should not be violated by any significant degree, or the structure is invalidated. The good test holds above it, on lighter volume.

reasons: which entry we teach is a held decision (D-003); keyed as the school's view

questions.q: Which range is the better place for a spring?
choices: A base after a long decline
A range right after an IPO
questions.why: A pause after a rise. The 60 sessions before the range rose, a reaccumulation pause, is preferred to a base after a decline.
questions.lesson_line: Prefer a pause after a rise to a base after a fall.

wrong.A base after a long decline: That is the classic accumulation spring. We prefer a pause after a rise.
wrong.A range under the 200-day: No longs under the 200-day unless a parabolic long.
wrong.A range right after an IPO: A new issue has no rise or floor history to read.

questions.q: Buy the spring?
questions.story: A textbook spring in a stock with an RS rating of 55, in a weak group.
questions.why: Skip. A spring is bought in a leader, RS 80 or more. Only parabolic and mean-reversion trades are exempt.
questions.lesson_line: No leader, no spring.

wrong.Buy; the shape is textbook: A textbook shape in a weak stock is still a pass.
wrong.Buy; springs are exempt: Only parabolic and mean-reversion trades are exempt from the leader rule.
wrong.Buy at half size: Size does not fix a weak stock.

questions.q: Can you take it?
choices: Buy it, it's a textbook spring
questions.story: A textbook spring in a stock trading under a flat 200-day, after a nine-month decline.
questions.why: Pass. Under the 200-day is a hard no for stocks, however clean the pattern looks. The only things we'll buy under that line are indexes and levered ETFs, on a reversal extension or a parabolic long. The springs we want sit in leaders resting after a run, not in stocks coming off a long slide. Put it on watch and come back if it gets back over the line.
questions.lesson_line: Under the 200-day, no stock long. The shape doesn't matter.

wrong.Buy it, it's a textbook spring: A textbook shape under the 200-day is still a no for a stock.
wrong.Buy half size, tight stop: Half size doesn't fix a hard no.
wrong.Pass until the 200-day rises: It's about where price sits, not the slope. Under the line is enough to pass.

questions.simple: Pass, because we don't buy stocks under the 200-day, however clean the spring looks.

deeper.trap: The trap is the textbook shape. After a long decline a spring can look perfect on its own chart. Our 200-day rule is hard for stocks: no long below the line. The shape never overrides the line.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26) beside the held D-009

questions.q: How would you grade it?
choices: Lower, the range is wide and loose
Full grade, the dip is shallow
Higher, a tall range is strong
Pass, too tall to be a spring
questions.story: A spring comes out of a flat range 30% tall. The dip is 0.4 ATR under the floor and closes back inside.
questions.answer: Lower, the range is wide and loose
questions.why: Lower. The dip itself is fine, 0.4 ATR and right back inside. But 30% from floor to top is a wide, loose range. I want tight. A range that wide tells you the stock swings hard, so the dip and your stop tend to run wider. It's still a spring, just not an A. Grading is my judgment, not a checklist.
questions.lesson_line: Tight ranges grade higher than wide, loose ones.

wrong.Full grade, the dip is shallow: The dip is fine, but a wide, loose range costs grade.
wrong.Higher, a tall range is strong: Tight ranges grade higher. Wide and loose grades lower.
wrong.Pass, too tall to be a spring: It's still a spring. A wide range costs grade, it doesn't rule it out.

questions.simple: Lower, because a wide loose range is weaker than a tight one, even with a clean dip.

deeper.trap: The trap is calling it a pass. A wide range costs grade, it doesn't throw the spring out. The 0.4 ATR dip is a clean one.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting the owner's review (20% height)
grading is discretionary (E50); the cue is credited to the card

questions.q: Name the setup.
questions.story: A stock dips just under its rising 50-day for a day and closes back above it. No flat range sits behind it.
questions.why: An undercut and rally. Name the level first. A spring's floor is a flat level with a range behind it. Here there's no range, just a rising 50-day. A dip under a rising average that closes back above it is a U&R. Both trap the people who sold under the level. The level tells you which setup you're trading.
questions.lesson_line: Flat floor, spring. Rising average, U&R.

wrong.A capitulation flush: A capitulation is a huge flush after a long fall. This barely dipped under the line.
wrong.A spring off the 50-day: A spring needs a flat floor with a range behind it. A rising average is a U&R level.
wrong.A 2B of one swing low: A 2B uses one swing low. Here the level is a rising average.

questions.simple: An undercut and rally, because the level is a rising 50-day, not a flat floor.

deeper.trap: The trap is calling every undercut a spring. Both dip under a level and close back above it. The difference is the level: a spring needs a flat floor with a range behind it, while a U&R can use a rising average, one swing low or a prior high.

reasons: rests on the card's lookalike tells (house)

questions.q: What did each trader just buy?
choices: A a spring, B a flat base
A a flat base, B a spring
questions.story: Two traders watch the same flat range. Trader A buys the reclaim at the floor after a dip under it. Trader B buys as price trades through the top.
questions.answer: A a spring, B a flat base
questions.why: A traded the spring, B the flat base. Same range, two setups. The spring buyer gets in at the floor, with the stop a few cents under the dip. The flat-base buyer gets in through the top, with the stop under the breakout day's low. Each one has its own stop, and that's the point. Don't buy at the top and leave your stop down at the floor.
questions.lesson_line: Floor reclaim, spring. Top breakout, flat base. Each gets its own stop.

wrong.A a flat base, B a spring: Other way round. The floor buy is the spring.
wrong.Both bought a spring: A spring is bought at the floor, not through the top.
wrong.Both bought a flat base: A flat base is bought through the top, not at the floor.

questions.simple: A bought the spring at the floor, and B bought the flat base through the top of the same range.

deeper.counter: Mixing them is the trap: buy over the top but keep the stop under the spring low. Now the stop is the whole range away, your size shrinks, and the reward for the risk is gone.

reasons: the reclaim entry is a held decision (D-003); keyed as the card's lookalike tell

questions.q: What would you call this?
questions.story: After a short pullback with no range behind it, a stock trades under the prior day's low. Same session, it closes back above the prior day's close.
questions.why: An Oops Reversal. It broke yesterday's low and took back yesterday's close on one candle. That's the Oops. A spring needs the floor of a range, a level the stock has held for weeks. This short pullback has no range behind it, just yesterday's low. Same kind of trap, different level, so you trade it by that setup's plan.
questions.lesson_line: Yesterday's low is an Oops. A range floor is a spring.

wrong.A spring low: A spring breaks the floor of a range. This only broke yesterday's low.
wrong.A capitulation: A capitulation is a huge flush after a long fall. This was a short pullback.
wrong.A failed break: A failed breakout is a break over a level that falls back. This broke a low.

questions.simple: An Oops Reversal, because it only broke yesterday's low, not the floor of a range.

reasons: rests on the card's lookalike tells (house)

questions.q: Which setup fits?
questions.story: A leader falls in a straight line. Then it drops 2.5 ATR in one day on twice its usual volume, under all its fast averages.
questions.why: A capitulation. A straight-line fall, then one huge flush on twice the usual volume, under every fast average. That's sellers giving up all at once. A spring is a small dip under a flat floor that snaps back. A 2.5 ATR drop in a day is no scratch, and there's no flat range here at all. Different setup, different plan.
questions.lesson_line: A huge flush after a straight fall is a capitulation, not a spring.

wrong.An Oops Reversal: An Oops breaks yesterday's low and takes back yesterday's close. Nothing here took anything back.
wrong.A shakeout spring: A shakeout still comes out of a flat range. This one's a straight fall and a huge flush.
wrong.An undercut and rally: A U&R dips under a level and rallies back. This was a straight-line flush.

questions.simple: A capitulation, because a 2.5 ATR flush on twice the volume after a straight fall is no small dip.

deeper.trap: Depth is the tell. A spring is a scratch under a flat floor. Deeper and sloppier, and it's a shakeout that grades lower. A one-day flush on heavy volume after a straight fall, with no range at all, is a capitulation, its own setup.

reasons: rests on the card's lookalike tells (house)

questions.q: What do you do now?
choices: You're out, the stop did its job
Buy it back bigger right away
Move the stop under the next low
Hold, it may close back inside
questions.story: February 2025. You bought a spring in a range 17.9% tall, after a 73% run. The same day it fell through your stop under the spring low.
questions.answer: You're out, the stop did its job
questions.why: You're out, and that's fine. The stop under the spring low was the plan, and it did its job. A spring that fails usually fails right away. In our study, 41% broke their low before any test came. Don't chase it back. Buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a new trade with its own stop. A tall range after a big run was the warning here.
questions.lesson_line: A stop-out is the cost of the setup. Take it and move on.

wrong.Move the stop under the next low: The stop only moves up, never lower. It was hit, so the trade is over.
wrong.Buy it back bigger right away: A new buy needs a new trigger, as a new trade with its own stop.
wrong.Hold, it may close back inside: The stop is the exit, and it was hit. It's a real order with your broker.

questions.simple: You're out, because the stop under the spring low was the plan, and it worked.

deeper.example: TSLA in our study: a 17.9% tall range after a 73% run. A tall range after a big run is a weaker spring. When it fails, the stop doing its job is the plan.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, B21)
fixed before (a dossier quote was wrong against the bars)

questions.q: How many R is the range top from your entry?
questions.why: 3R. Your risk is 142.00 minus 140.00, 2 a share. The top is 148.00 minus 142.00, 6 above you. 6 over 2 is 3.0R. That's why I like buying the shakeout. By the time the breakout buyers step in at the top, you're already up 3-1 on your risk. The top is the first place sellers can show up, so know that number before you buy.
questions.lesson_line: Buy the shakeout, and you're up 3-1 before the breakout buyers show up.
questions.simple: 3R, because the 2 of risk fits three times into the 6 up to the 148.00 top.

deeper.counter: Here the top is close. When it's only 3R away, the first resistance and 3R arrive together. That's a fine spot to think about a first sell, if it's day 3 or later.

reasons: rests on house sources (the DELL plan, the card)

wrong.6.0R: That's the dollar climb, 6. You still divide it by the 2 of risk.
wrong.4.0R: You measured from the stop, not your entry.
wrong.0.3R: Flipped the division, risk over the climb.

questions.story: DELL. Our plan: a shakeout to 140.00, then buy the reclaim of 142.00 with the stop at 140.00. The old range top is 148.00.

questions.q: In our scan of 3,173 springs, about what share reached 3R before the stop?
questions.why: About a quarter: 27.1% reached 3R and 17.7% reached 5R, and 83.8% were stopped within the window. That is a fixed stop with no trims.
questions.lesson_line: A quarter got to 3R. The stop is the trade.

questions.q: Write the plan. Entry, stop, first sell?
questions.story: May 2023. A flat shelf runs from 60.32 to 64.85. A quiet one-day dip, 0.15 ATR under the floor, closes back inside. The next open is 61.59.
questions.why: Buy the open at 61.59, stop at 60.10, and no selling before day 3. The dip went under the 60.32 floor, so the stop goes a few cents under the dip's low, not on the floor. That's 60.10. It keeps your risk tight, which is the whole reason to buy a spring. The first sell is a judgment, from day 3 at the earliest, into a push.
questions.lesson_line: Entry at the reclaim, stop under the spring low, first sell from day 3.

wrong.Over 64.85, stop 60.32, sell at top: That's the breakout over the top, and 60.32 is the old floor, above the spring low.
wrong.61.59, stop 60.32, hold a month: 60.32 is the old floor, above the spring low. The stop goes a few cents under the dip.
wrong.Over 64.85, stop 60.10, sell day 3: That buys over the top but keeps the stop down under the floor. The stop is now the whole range away.

questions.simple: Buy 61.59 at the open, stop just under the spring low at 60.10, and sell from day 3.

deeper.trap: The trap is the breakout plan. Buy over the top at 64.85 with the stop still under the spring low, and your stop is the whole range wide. The spring's edge is the low-risk buy at the floor.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E57, F62, B19)

questions.q: Take it or pass, on the pattern alone?
choices: Take it, flat floor, modest dip
Pass, the dip is a breakdown
Take it, the volume was heavy
questions.answer: Take it, flat floor, modest dip
questions.why: I'd take it. Five taps of the floor make it a real level. The probe went three-quarters of an ATR under, a bit deeper than a scratch. Then it closed right back inside, a hammer. That's buyers stepping in at the floor, a good look. Volume was 0.96x, about normal, so nobody was dumping it. Taking it means it's worth a plan: buy the reclaim, stop a few cents under the low.
questions.lesson_line: Judge the snap back, not the drama of the dip.

wrong.Pass, there's no range here: Look again. The floor was tapped five times.
wrong.Pass, the dip is a breakdown: A breakdown keeps going. This one closed back inside the same day.
wrong.Take it, the volume was heavy: Volume was 0.96x, about normal. The floor and the snap back make this one.

questions.simple: Take it. The floor is real, and the 0.75 ATR dip closed back inside as a hammer.

deeper.trap: The trap is the deeper probe. After five taps, three-quarters of an ATR under can look like a break. It closed back in on normal volume, and that's a spring.

reasons: rests on our own scan's example, not yet reviewed by the owner

questions.story: October 2021. A flat range 7.2% tall, floor tapped five times. Today it probes 0.75 ATR under the floor, then closes back inside on 0.96x volume.

questions.q: Spring or pass?
choices: Pass, one swing low is a 2B
Take it, the dip was shallow
Take it, the floor is flat
Pass, that low is too old
questions.answer: Pass, one swing low is a 2B
questions.why: Pass, as a spring at least. One swing low isn't a floor. A spring needs a flat range, a level the stock tested again and again. Here price touched once, then ran 14% away. Undercut one swing low and reclaim it, and that's a 2B, a different setup with its own plan. Look left first: no range, no spring.
questions.lesson_line: Look left first. No range, no spring.

wrong.Take it, the dip was shallow: A shallow dip doesn't make a floor. A spring needs a flat range.
wrong.Take it, the floor is flat: There's no flat floor here, just one swing low.
wrong.Pass, that low is too old: Age isn't the problem. The level is one swing low, and that's a 2B.

questions.simple: Pass, because one old swing low makes a 2B, and a spring needs a flat floor.

deeper.trap: The trap is a clean undercut. The dip was shallow and closed back above the low, just like a spring. But the level was one swing low that price rallied 14% off, with no flat range behind it. Look left first: no range, no spring.

reasons: tied to the held floor-touch decision D-112

questions.story: August 2021. The floor is one swing low from 40 sessions ago, and price rallied 14% off it. Today it undercuts that low and closes back above.

questions.q: What does Wyckoff's step 5 ask of the buyer?
choices: Time your buy with a turn in the index
questions.answer: Time your buy with a turn in the index
questions.why: Time your commitment with a turn in the stock market index. Springs work best when the index itself has just sprung back.
questions.lesson_line: Wait for the index to turn.

wrong.Buy before the index turns: Step 5 says to time your buy with the turn, not ahead of it.
wrong.Ignore the index: The index matters. A failed index spring takes leaders with it.
wrong.Buy only on a Monday: Nothing in the step mentions a weekday.

questions.q: Taylor says the spring low should not be violated by any significant degree.
questions.why: True. In his view the spring low should not be violated by any significant degree, or the structure is invalidated.
questions.lesson_line: A spring that breaks its low is invalid.

questions.q: Pruden calls the spring the first place to buy. What does he say is better?
questions.why: The later secondary test. Pruden says the spring is the first prescribed place to buy and the secondary test is better.
questions.lesson_line: A quiet test can beat the spring itself.

wrong.The breakout over the top: Wyckoff says not to buy breakouts.
wrong.The selling climax: The test comes after the spring, not at a climax.
wrong.Waiting a year: The test comes in the following days or weeks.

questions.q: Which candidate grades higher?
choices: A; the range, dip and close are cleaner
B; the deeper dip shook out more
questions.story: A: a range 8% tall, a dip of 0.3 ATR, a reclaim that closes in the upper half. B: a range 24% tall, a dip of 1.4 ATR, a reclaim that closes mid-range.
questions.answer: A; the range, dip and close are cleaner
questions.why: A. A range over 20% tall grades lower. A dip over 1 ATR is a shakeout that grades lower. A good reclaim closes in the upper half.
questions.lesson_line: Short range, shallow dip, strong close: the higher grade.

wrong.B; the deeper dip shook out more: A dip over 1 ATR is a shakeout, and it grades lower.
wrong.They grade the same: Range height, dip depth and close quality all separate them.
wrong.Neither; both are breakdowns: A breakdown is over 2 ATR. Neither dip is that deep.

questions.q: Does the index make this one better or worse?
choices: No change, only the stock counts
Worse, the bounce is used up
questions.story: A leader springs off a flat range floor. Last week the index dipped under its correction low and closed back above it. Our market reading is Green.
questions.why: Better. Last week's dip and close back above the low was the index's own spring. Wyckoff's step is to time your buy with a turn in the market index. Here you have it. The market just sprang, the reading is Green, and a leader is springing with it. That's the kind I want to press. When the market and the leader turn together, you're not fighting anything.
questions.lesson_line: A leader's spring with the index turning too, that's one to press.

wrong.No change, only the stock counts: The index matters. A spring works best with the market turning too.
wrong.Worse, the index is correcting: The index just sprang back off its correction low. That's the turn.
wrong.Worse, the bounce is used up: An index that just sprang is a fresh turn, not a late one.

questions.simple: Better, because the index just sprang too and the reading is Green, so the market is behind you.

questions.q: Does the run before this range help or hurt?
choices: Helps, it's a pause after a rise
Hurts, a fall before is better
Hurts, it's too late to buy now
questions.story: August 2025. A flat range 13.5% tall follows a 31% run. Today it dips under the floor and closes back inside.
questions.answer: Helps, it's a pause after a rise
questions.why: It helps. A leader that ran 31% and then went sideways is resting, not topping. Fraser calls a range like that a stepping stone. The spring shakes out the weak hands before the next leg. A base after a long decline is the other kind, and those often sit under the 200-day, where we don't buy stocks. HWM went on to 16.5R at its best.
questions.lesson_line: I want a pause after a run, not a base after a fall.

wrong.Hurts, a fall before is better: A base after a fall often sits under the 200-day. We want a pause in a leader.
wrong.Doesn't matter either way: It matters. A pause after a run is the spring we're after.
wrong.Hurts, it's too late to buy now: A prior run is the good setting, not a reason to pass.

questions.simple: It helps, because a flat pause after a run in a leader is the spring we want.

deeper.example: HWM: a stepping-stone range after a 31% run, three floor touches and a shallow quiet probe. The range ran from 170.34 to 193.26, 13.5% tall. The buy was 171.85 with the stop at 169.42, and it reached 16.5R at best.

questions.q: When does the stop go to breakeven on a spring?
choices: At the first trim, by default
questions.answer: At the first trim, by default
questions.why: At the first trim by default, and anywhere between 2R and 5R. The first sell is a judgment, not a fixed third at 3R.
questions.lesson_line: Breakeven comes with the first trim.

wrong.Never: The stop moves to breakeven between 2R and 5R.
wrong.Before the buy: There is no position yet. Breakeven comes after the first trim.
wrong.At the open each day: The stop only moves up when the rule says so, not each day.

questions.q: What type is this, and what next?
choices: A number 2 spring; wait for the test
questions.story: The dip goes much further under the low on expanded volume. Then it lifts briefly and drops back toward the lows.
questions.answer: A number 2 spring; wait for the test
questions.why: A number 2 spring. It goes further below the low on expanded volume, then lifts and drops back for a test. High volume springs need to be tested first.
questions.lesson_line: A deeper, louder spring waits for its test.

wrong.A number 3 spring; buy now: A number 3 spring is shallow on modest volume. This one is deeper and louder.
wrong.A number 1 spring; buy now: A number 1 spring is a complete breakdown, and it should not be bought.
wrong.A breakout; add: The stock dipped under the low. A breakout goes over the top.

questions.q: Four valid springs lost. Which one had no warning sign?
choices: TSLA; a tall range after a run
questions.why: MSFT. It met every rule and was stopped on the entry day. GOOGL's market, AAPL's index and TSLA's 17.9% range after a 73% run were warnings.
questions.lesson_line: Some good springs still fail. The stop is the trade.

wrong.GOOGL; the market was weak: It was not a Green market, a warning sign.
wrong.AAPL; the index failed: QQQ sprang the same day and failed too, a warning sign.
wrong.TSLA; a tall range after a run: A 17.9% range after a 73% run was a warning sign.

questions.q: Your spring has pushed up to the top of its range. Wyckoff traders then watch for a back-up. What is it?
choices: A light dip that holds the old top
A heavy drop back under the floor
The first dip under the floor
A gap up through the range top
questions.answer: A light dip that holds the old top
questions.why: A light pullback that holds the old top. After the push, price backs off on lighter volume, and the old ceiling acts as support. Pruden describes it as a narrow reaction on lighter volume that confirms the jump. What it tells you is that the push was real. Don't mix it up with the spring, which dips under the floor.
questions.lesson_line: After the push, a quiet pullback that holds the old top is the back-up.

wrong.The first dip under the floor: That's the spring itself. The back-up comes later, after the push.
wrong.A heavy drop back under the floor: That's a failure, not a back-up. A back-up is light and holds the old top.
wrong.A gap up through the range top: That's the push. The back-up is the pullback after it.

questions.simple: The back-up is the first light pullback after the push that holds the old top.

questions.q: Fraser calls this a classic place to add. What do you do?
choices: Just hold, adding isn't the plan
Add half size, keep the same stop
Double up and raise the stop
Sell it, the pullback is a warning
questions.answer: Just hold, adding isn't the plan
questions.why: Just hold. Fraser and ChartSchool both call this a place to add. We don't plan it. We buy the full size at one price with one stop, and that's the position. Adding to a working winner on strength does happen, but it's rare and a feel call, never the plan. A light pullback that holds the old top is a good sign, so sit on your hands.
questions.lesson_line: Wyckoff adds at the back-up. We buy once and let it work.

wrong.Add half size, keep the same stop: That's the textbook add. For us adding is never the plan. The full size went on once.
wrong.Double up and raise the stop: Doubling up is the textbook's plan. We buy once and let it work.
wrong.Sell it, the pullback is a warning: A light pullback that holds the old top is support showing up. The stop is your exit.

questions.story: You hold a long from the spring. The stock has pushed to the top of the range and now pulls back on light volume, holding the old top.
questions.simple: Just hold. We buy the full size once, and adding is never part of the plan.

deeper.trap: Where the textbook and our rules split, our rules win. Fraser and ChartSchool add here. We buy once, at one price with one stop.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A5) over a web view

questions.q: Can you trade it?
choices: Yes, the dollar volume is big
Half size, it's a tight range
No, 60 million a day is too low
questions.why: No. We only trade stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day. This one clears the dollar volume easily at about 60 million. But 9.40 is under the $10 line, so it's a pass. Both have to clear. Miss either one and it doesn't go on your list.
questions.lesson_line: Two floors: $10 a share and $20 million a day. Miss either, pass.

wrong.Yes, the dollar volume is big: Both floors have to clear. The price is under $10.
wrong.Half size, it's a tight range: Half size doesn't waive a floor.
wrong.No, 60 million a day is too low: 60 million clears our 20 million floor. The price is the problem.

questions.story: A clean spring shows up in a 9.40 stock that trades about 60 million dollars a day.
questions.simple: No, because 9.40 is under our $10 floor, even though the volume is fine.

questions.q: A stock with a clean spring trades 750,000 shares a day at 24.00. How much is that in dollars a day?
questions.why: $18 million a day. Shares times price: 750,000 times 24.00 is 18,000,000. That's under our $20 million floor, so it's off the list, however good the chart looks. A thin stock is hard to get out of when you need to. Check dollar volume before you even look at the pattern.
questions.lesson_line: Check dollar volume before the pattern.
questions.simple: $18 million a day, which is under our $20 million floor, so it's off the list.

wrong.$180,000,000: The decimal point slipped a place.
wrong.$432,000,000: You multiplied by the price twice.

questions.q: Apart from a gap through it, your stop on a spring only ever moves up.
questions.why: True. The stop is your exit. It moves up as the trade works, never down or wider. The one exception is a gap. On a gap through the stop, the first 30-minute low becomes your new stop, and you're out if that's past 2R. Lowering a stop because price is close to it is how a small loss turns into a big one.
questions.lesson_line: A stop moves up, never down. A gap is the one exception.
questions.simple: True, a stop only moves up, except when a gap opens below it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, B20)

questions.q: What do you do with the stop?
choices: Leave it at 51.10, it stays put
Drop it to 50.20 to give it room
Cancel it and watch the close
Widen it and sell some shares
questions.answer: Leave it at 51.10, it stays put
questions.why: Leave it at 51.10. Your size came from 52.40 and 51.10. Drop the stop to 50.20 and you're risking more than you planned, on a trade that's going against you. The stop only moves up. Keep it as a real order with your broker, not a level you watch. If the spring fails, it fails fast, and the stop is what gets you out.
questions.lesson_line: Leave the stop alone. It moves up, never down.

wrong.Drop it to 50.20 to give it room: A stop never goes lower. Your size already came from 51.10.
wrong.Cancel it and watch the close: The stop is a real order with your broker, not a close you watch.
wrong.Widen it and sell some shares: Cutting shares doesn't make a lower stop okay. After the buy, it only moves up.

questions.story: You bought a spring at 52.40 with a real stop order at 51.10. The stock sags to 51.60 and you feel like dropping the stop to 50.20.
questions.simple: Leave the stop at 51.10, because after the buy a stop only moves up, never lower.

deeper.trap: Cutting shares to widen the stop feels like the same risk. It is not the plan. The size came from the honest stop at the buy, and after the entry the stop only moves up. A spring that fails usually fails at once, so the old stop is doing its job.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, D41)

questions.q: On a spring trade, it's fine to move your stop to breakeven at your first sell.
questions.why: True. We move the stop to breakeven somewhere between 2R and 5R, or at the first sell. When you've just sold some into strength, that's a natural time to do it. Now the rest of the trade can't turn into a loss. When exactly is a judgment. Too early, and a normal pullback takes you out at zero.
questions.lesson_line: Breakeven between 2R and 5R, or at the first sell.
questions.simple: True. At the first sell, moving the stop to breakeven means the rest can't become a loss.

questions.q: Where's 2R, the earliest spot you'd think about breakeven?
questions.why: 176.71. Your risk is 171.85 minus 169.42, which is 2.43 a share. Two of those is 4.86. Add that to 171.85 and you get 176.71. That's where our breakeven window opens. It runs from 2R to 5R, or the first sell. Know the number before the open, so you're not doing math with the stock moving.
questions.lesson_line: Know your 2R before the open.
questions.simple: 2R is 176.71, the buy plus twice the 2.43 of risk.

wrong.$181.57: Two R too many. You doubled the 2R.
wrong.$184.00: That's 5R, the far end of the window.

questions.story: August 2025. You bought at 171.85 with the stop at 169.42.

questions.q: You bought 900 shares of a spring. You sold 300 into the first push and 300 into a later one. How many are left to trail?
questions.why: 300. You've sold 300 and 300, so 600 are gone. 900 minus 600 leaves 300 to trail. How much you sell, and when, is a judgment, so these are just example numbers. What's left rides under the 20 EMA, or the 9 EMA if it's fast, until a close below it.
questions.lesson_line: Whatever you sell, trail what's left.
questions.simple: 300 are left, because two sells of 300 come off the 900.

wrong.100 shares: That sells far too much. Two sells of 300 leave 300.
wrong.200 shares: That counts one sell as bigger than 300.
wrong.150 shares: That halves the 300 left. There's no third sell here.

questions.q: What's the plan from here?
choices: Weigh a later sell, trail the rest
Sell everything and lock it in
Add back what you already sold
Sell a fixed third, trail the rest
questions.answer: Weigh a later sell, trail the rest
questions.why: Weigh another sell and trail the rest. Later sells are a judgment, like the first. Selling at about 5 to 10R is often best, so 5R is a fine spot to think about it. But no fixed third comes off at 5R. Whatever's left trails under the 9 EMA if it's fast, or the 20 EMA if it's steady. And you don't buy back what you sold.
questions.lesson_line: Sell into strength by judgment. Trail what's left.

wrong.Sell everything and lock it in: That ends a trade that's still working. Sell part by judgment and trail the rest.
wrong.Add back what you already sold: Buying back what you sold isn't the plan. The trail handles the rest.
wrong.Sell a fixed third, trail the rest: No fixed third comes off at 5R. Later sells are a judgment too.

questions.story: Your spring buy has made its first sell. Price now touches 5R and the stop is at breakeven.
questions.simple: Weigh a later sell and trail the rest, because later sells are a judgment, not a fixed third.

deeper.trap: The trap is to sell a fixed third at 5R. A later sell is a judgment, and what is left trails under a rising average.

questions.q: On a spring, you sell when price reaches its Wyckoff point-and-figure target.
questions.why: False. A Wyckoff count is a place to stop, look and listen, not an exit. ChartSchool says those targets should never be treated as exact turning points. We sell into strength by judgment and trail the rest under the 20 EMA or the 9 EMA. If price nears a count, pay attention to how it acts there. That's all.
questions.lesson_line: A Wyckoff target is a place to look and listen, not an exit.
questions.simple: False. A Wyckoff target is only a place to look and listen, and we sell by judgment.

questions.q: Wyckoff traders project how far a stock can run out of its range. What do they measure that with?
questions.why: The point-and-figure count. That's the Wyckoff tool for it. ChartSchool says the cause a range builds is measured by the horizontal count on a point-and-figure chart. The bigger the range, the bigger the cause, and the bigger the move it can feed. Pruden uses those counts for his projections too. Twice the range height looks like Wyckoff, but no Wyckoff source uses it. For us even a real count is a place to look and listen, not a sell order.
questions.lesson_line: Wyckoff measures the run with the point-and-figure count.

wrong.Twice the range's height: Some scanners use it, but no Wyckoff source does.
wrong.A fixed 3R on every trade: 3R is our yardstick for risk, not Wyckoff's objective. And our first sell is a judgment.
wrong.The prior all-time high: Wyckoff's objectives come from the count, not a prior high.

questions.simple: The point-and-figure count, which measures how much cause a range has built.

deeper.trap: Twice the range height shows up on some scanners, but no Wyckoff source uses it. Even the real count is a place to stop, look and listen.
